opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few separate reasons, and they compound.

The first is just the measurement itself. The time horizon number comes from a particular suite of tasks: mostly software engineering, research engineering, and some cybersecurity-flavored things. We estimate how long those tasks take skilled humans, and then we fit a curve to where models succeed at, say, 50% of the time. Every piece of that has noise. Human baseline times vary a lot depending on who you ask and how familiar they are with the codebase. Our task distribution gets thinner at the long end, so the estimates for the most capable models rest on fewer, harder-to-baseline tasks. So even the slope, the doubling time, has real error bars, and when you extrapolate an exponential a few years out, small differences in the slope turn into huge differences in where you end up.

The second is a question of what the number means outside our tasks. Our tasks are fairly well specified, automatically scorable, and relatively "clean" compared to real work. Real work is messy: underspecified goals, lots of context you have to pick up, coordinating with other people, no clear signal of whether you've succeeded. We've done some work looking at messiness factors, and models do somewhat worse on messier tasks. So it's not obvious that a two-hour time horizon on our suite corresponds to being able to do two hours of a typical person's job. The trend might transfer, or the gap might stay roughly constant, or it might widen. We don't really know yet.

The third is whether the trend itself continues. An exponential fit over the last several years is a description of the past, not a law. It's driven by underlying inputs: compute scaling, algorithmic progress, more investment in agentic training and RL, better scaffolding. Some of those could slow down, because compute buildouts face physical and financial constraints. Some could speed up. If AI systems start meaningfully accelerating AI research itself, you could get a faster-than-exponential regime. We've actually seen hints that the doubling time recently has been shorter than the longer-run average, and it's hard to tell whether that's a real regime change or noise in a few data points.

And then finally there's the step from "time horizon" to the thing people actually care about forecasting, like economic impact or automation of AI R&D or particular dangerous capabilities. That mapping isn't something the metric gives you directly. You need extra assumptions, like how much of a job decomposes into tasks of what length, or how reliability at 80% or 95% compares to 50%. Those assumptions can matter as much as the trend itself.

So I'd say the trend is one of the more useful quantitative handles we have, and it's been surprisingly robust. But I'd be pretty cautious about anyone who takes the line, extends it out, and reads off a confident date for something transformative.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about whether the trend continues, citing compute constraints, algorithmic progress, investment, and possible AI-driven research acceleration. It does not identify a change in AI paradigms as a reason the trend may fail to predict future progress.

r002.rationale: It names compute scaling, algorithmic progress, investment in agentic training and RL, and scaffolding as drivers, but does not say the observed exponential time-horizon growth may reflect exponential growth in training resources.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on. The first is just that the measurement itself is noisier than it looks. The time horizon number comes from taking a set of tasks, estimating how long they'd take a human expert, and then finding the length at which a model succeeds about half the time. Every piece of that is kind of soft. The human baselines are often from a handful of people, the tasks are mostly self-contained software engineering problems, and the fifty percent threshold is somewhat arbitrary. If you move to an eighty percent success threshold, the horizons shrink a lot, and the doubling time changes too. So the headline curve is really a curve about one particular slice of task space under one particular definition of success.

The second thing is that the tasks on the benchmark aren't a random sample of what people actually do with their time. They're chosen partly because they're measurable, which means they have clear specifications and automatic grading. Real work has a lot of ambiguity, a lot of context that lives in people's heads, a lot of "the thing you were asked for isn't actually the thing that's needed." It's possible that models get better at the clean, well-specified tasks much faster than at the messy ones, and the time horizon metric mostly tracks the former. So even if the exponential continues on the benchmark, it's not obvious what that implies for the economy or for the kinds of research tasks people care about from a safety perspective.

And then the third thing, which I think is the most important, is that extrapolating an exponential assumes the underlying drivers stay the same. The trend we've seen is a mix of scaling compute, improving training methods, better post-training, and better scaffolding. Some of those are going to run into limits. Compute can't double forever at the same price, and some of the gains have come from relatively cheap fixes that you only get to use once. Other drivers might accelerate, like if models start contributing meaningfully to AI research. So you have a trend line that's the sum of several different processes, and the honest answer is we don't know which of them dominate going forward. Fitting a line through seven or eight points and extending it five years out is the kind of thing that works until it doesn't.

I want to be clear that I don't think the metric is useless. It's one of the better attempts we have to put a number on something that's otherwise very hand-wavy. I just think the error bars on the forecast should be much wider than the clean plot suggests, in both directions.

r001.rationale: The response says the trend combines several drivers that may slow or accelerate, but it does not identify a possible change in AI paradigms as a reason the trend may fail to predict future progress.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difficulty is figuring out what that trend is actually measuring, and how it maps onto the things we care about. A task’s time horizon usually means something like how long it takes a human to complete it. But tasks that take humans the same amount of time can have very different levels of difficulty for an AI. So doubling that number doesn’t necessarily mean doubling the length of a project an AI can autonomously carry out.

There’s also a big difference between succeeding on a task some fraction of the time and being reliable enough that you can delegate it. You might get a fairly clean exponential trend at one success threshold, but the economically relevant question could depend on a much higher threshold, or on how much human supervision is needed.

And then you have to extrapolate beyond the kinds of tasks you’ve measured. Longer projects can involve ambiguity, discovering what needs to be done, and interacting with the world, rather than just executing a well-specified assignment. I think the trend is useful evidence. But turning it into a forecast requires assumptions about whether those additional difficulties will be overcome at the same rate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task difficulty, reliability, supervision, and extrapolation to longer projects, but it does not identify possible changes in AI paradigms as a reason the trend may stop predicting progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main difficulty is that there are several steps between observing an exponential trend on a benchmark and forecasting something like when AI can automate a large fraction of research.

The time horizon is usually measured in terms of how long a task takes a human. But that’s not necessarily a consistent measure of how difficult it is for an AI. A task that takes a human eight hours might involve doing a fairly straightforward thing repeatedly, or it might involve one really difficult insight. Those could have very different trajectories. So it matters a lot which tasks are in your evaluation, and whether they’re representative of the work you actually care about.

And then there’s reliability. Being able to complete a task half the time is useful evidence about capability, but it doesn’t immediately tell you whether a system can work autonomously for weeks. Perhaps you can close that gap with retries and verification, but perhaps the failures are correlated or difficult to detect.

So I do think the trend is informative. I’m just more uncertain about the mapping from that trend to economically important capabilities than a clean exponential curve might suggest.
